front.title: Grow a lump sum
front.html:
⟨A=P\left(1+\dfrac{r}{m}\right)^{mt}⟩
P = initial dollars; A = ending dollars; r = nominal annual decimal return; m = compounds per year; t = years.
$1,000 at a hypothetical 6%, annually for 10 years:
⟨1{,}000(1.06)^{10}\approx1{,}790.85⟩
About $1,790.85
No deposits, fees or taxes; a constant return is a model, not a promise.

front.title: Regular deposits
front.html:
⟨F=D\dfrac{(1+i)^N-1}{i}⟩
D = dollars deposited at each period’s end; i = decimal return per period; N = deposit count; F = future dollars.
For monthly deposits: ⟨i=\tfrac{r}{12}⟩, ⟨N=12t⟩.
Assumes no initial balance, fixed return, no fees or tax. At 0% return, ⟨F=DN⟩.
Beginning-of-period deposits grow one extra period: multiply by ⟨1+i⟩.

front.title: Long-term deposit example
front.text: Hypothetical 7% nominal annual return, monthly compounding; month-end deposits; no fees or tax.

front.title: Deposit needed for a goal
front.html:
⟨D=\dfrac{Fi}{(1+i)^N-1}⟩
F = goal in future dollars; i = decimal return per period; N = deposits.
Goal $10,000; 60 month-end deposits; hypothetical 6% nominal return:
⟨D=\dfrac{10{,}000(0.005)}{(1.005)^{60}-1}⟩
About $143.33 monthly
No starting balance, fees or tax; plan extra margin because actual returns vary.

front.title: Match risk to the goal
head: Need the money
What to consider
rows: Accessible cash or suitable insured deposits.
Balance growth potential with possible losses.
Diversified investments may fit; losses still occur.
front.after: Time horizon, ability to absorb loss and willingness to take risk all matter. A long horizon does not guarantee a gain.

back.title: Which fund costs less?
back.text: Same gross 7% return assumed, 20 years, $10,000 initial; approximate net return = gross − annual fee. No tax; difference uses unrounded balances.

back.title: Compare beyond the fee
back.html:
The fee comparison favors A if risk, holdings and services are otherwise equal. Ask what each fund owns and whether advice or restrictions differ.
Expense ratio: annual fund cost as a percent of assets.
0.2% of $10,000 = $20 for one year at a constant balance.
Small recurring costs can compound into a large difference. Compare like with like.

back.title: Return & purchasing power
back.html:
⟨\text{Return}=\dfrac{\text{end}-\text{start}}{\text{start}}⟩
No added or withdrawn cash; add distributions to the ending value when measuring total return.
⟨\text{Real return}=\dfrac{1+r}{1+f}-1⟩
r = nominal return; f = inflation, both annual decimals.
7% return, 3% inflation:
⟨\tfrac{1.07}{1.03}-1\approx3.88\%⟩ real gain.
Subtracting inflation is only an approximation.

back.title: A loss needs a bigger gain
back.text: Percent changes apply to the new balance, not always the original amount.

back.title: Rule of 72
back.html:
Approximate doubling time:
⟨\text{years}\approx\dfrac{72}{\text{annual rate in percent}}⟩
At hypothetical 6% growth:
⟨\tfrac{72}{6}=12⟩ years (approximate).
Exact factor after 12 years: ⟨1.06^{12}\approx2.012⟩.
Use 6 in the shortcut, not 0.06. Best as a rough estimate for moderate positive rates; actual market paths differ.

back.title: Reminders & mistakes
good: State return, deposit timing, fees and time period.
Keep money for near-term essential needs accessible.
